We gave ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Claude the same 10 shopping messages to see whether AI could tell a scam from a legitimate transaction.

external.description:
key takeaways

  * All four assistants caught all five scam-control messages.
  * ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude correctly cleared all five legitimate controls; Copilot marked two as uncertain.
  * Scam-risk scores ranged from 78 to 95, while legitimate controls ranged from 5 to 40, with no overlap in this controlled test.
  * AI was most useful for spotting red flags and suggesting checks, not for proving that a seller is genuine.



Imagine you are about to transfer ₦300,000 to an online seller.

The price looks reasonable, but something feels off. The seller wants a bank transfer. Perhaps they are rushing you, the account name doesn't match the business, or they say you cannot inspect the item before paying.

But before pressing send, would pasting that message you receive from said seller into an AI assistant help you determine if you’re about to get scammed?

That matters because AI is already entering the same shopping journey where many Nigerians encounter fraud. Visa's 2026 Stay Secure study found that 88% of Nigerian consumers surveyed used AI to assist with shopping, while 83% bought products through social media. Among respondents who had experienced scams, 57% said it happened on social media.

So, I tested whether four popular AI assistants could recognise warning signs before money changed hands.

**MORE INSIGHTS ON THIS TOPIC:**

record.text: A simple piece of tape could previously hide Meta's recording indicator. The company is now making the camera shut down when it detects the light has been covered or tampered with.

external.description:
Covertly recording people with smart glasses without their permission has become a growing concern. When Meta launched its first-generation Ray-Ban Stories, the company added a recording LED to let people nearby know when the glasses were capturing photos or videos.

But users soon found a way around it: simply covering the recording light with tape could allow the glasses to look like an ordinary pair of glasses while still recording.

Meta is now moving to close that loophole. The company says its AI glasses will disable the camera when they detect that the capture LED has been blocked or physically tampered with. Meta has also been improving its ability to detect attempts to modify or destroy the LED.

Meta Smart Glasses App May Contain Unreleased Face Recognition CodeA report found a code hidden inside Meta’s smart glasses app, reviving questions about consent, surveillance, and privacy.TechloyOgbonda Chivumnovu

## Why Meta is making the change

The reasoning is fairly simple. As AI glasses become more popular, concerns about people using them to secretly record others are growing.

There have been cases of people using smart glasses to covertly film and harass others in public. Back in February, Techloy reported on Russian man Vladislav Liulkov, who had been accused by the governments of Kenya and Ghana of secretly recording women without their consent, editing the clips, and posting them online.

Instagram has also taken action against creators who post this type of content, but the problem has continued.

There is another problem Meta is trying to address: a market for accessories and services designed to bypass the recording light.
